en: The steadfast King Harihara, a protective jewel for the lineage of the illustrious Rukmimahīpāla, guards the earth girt by the oceans. 1.
That king, who was learned in all the tantras, having worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the bestower of boons,
praised him with hymns known by all the Vedas.
Viṣṇu, his heart gladdened by that praise and surrounded by the cowherd women,
revealed his form, dark as a peacock feather and adorned with a crest of peacock feathers.
Then, having consecrated King Hariharā with showers of compassion while his mind was fixed upon his own self, he spoke to the king who stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Know me, O highly fortunate one, best among those who know what must be done, to be Kṛṣṇa standing before you through your devotion; may all your heart's desires be fulfilled. (5)
For the protection of the virtuous, for the punishment of the wicked,
and for the prosperity of the Vedas and the Dharma, my partial incarnation (aṃśatva) is proclaimed here.
O King, Rāma has been praised by you with this thousand names;
therefore, as one who knows all things, I am especially pleased with him.
O illustrious one, please also gratify me by reciting a thousand names that grant all desires, which are identical in essence to my own deeds.
This has been clearly elucidated in a hymn by the sage Parāśara, by Vyāsa the seer of the traditional scriptures, and also by Śuka, who was absorbed in his own self.
Therefore, you must seek out that thousand-headed Lord;
he will protect the thousand [seeds] entrusted by me to others.
For the sake of the welfare of the world, you must reveal this, which is approved by the supreme scriptures, upon the earth as a performance for the stage of the tongue. 11.
This should never be disclosed to one who is deceitful, foolish, an atheist, dissolute, envious, or even harmful.
To one who is discerning, pure, following the path of the Vedas,
a believer, established in the Self, and who has realized the rising [of the light] within his own soul.
One of purified intellect should indeed recite this Thousand Names of Kṛṣṇa.
The application (viniyoga) is: Oṃ, of this mantra of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sahasranāma-stotra, Parāśara is the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;

"Śrī Kṛṣṇa" is the seed-syllable (bīja); "Śrī Vallabha" is the power (śakti); "Śārṅgin" is the pin (kīlaka); and the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of recitation (japa) for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Obeisance to the seer Parāśara"— thus on the head;
"Obeisance to the Anuṣṭubh meter"— thus on the mouth.
"Salutation to the deity Gopālakṛṣṇa," thus at the heart;
"Salutation to Śrīkṛṣṇa, the seed-syllable," thus at the secret place; "Salutation to the power (śakti) of Śrīvallabha," thus at the feet.
"Obeisance to Śārṅgadhara, the Kīlaka," [recite] for all the limbs.
The *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment):
from "Śrīkṛṣṇa" up to "śūravaṃśaikadhīḥ," [assign] "namaḥ to both thumbs.
From "śauriḥ" up to "svabhāsodbhāsitavrajaḥ," [assign] "namaḥ to both index fingers."
Beginning with "Having established the arrangement of self-knowledge" up to "mounted upon the carriage of the [spiritual] path," salutation to the middle fingers;
beginning with "having made his abode in Vṛndāvana" up to "beheld by the King of Madhurā," salutation to the ring fingers;
and beginning with "the repeller of the washerman" up to "the fashioning of the city of Dvārakā," salutation to the little fingers.

Beginning with "Dvārakānilaya" and ending with "Parāśara," one should perform the placement [of mantras] on the palms and the backs of the hands; in this same manner, the placement on the heart and other parts [of the body] is performed.
Meditation:
for some men of love whose minds have dissolved, it is the playful sport of childhood; for others, it is the Lord whose body is marked by the pastimes of a cowherd, playing the flute.

Victorious is that Lord of the worlds who, having perceived that their desires were thus divided—knowing that the God of Love had been aroused in them at the assembly of the gods and that he was the very remover of the pride of the Daityas—became such [as he is]. || 1 ||
Having been praised by the hosts of gods, Brahmā, and other wise ones in the Ocean of Milk,
He was joyfully born in the house of Vasudeva and played in Gokula; for the sake of destroying Kaṃsa, He went to Mathurā and to the excellent Dvārakā with Rukmiṇī.
May that Gopāla, the friend of all the cowherd girls, protect us from calamity. || 2 ||
With the splendor of a full-blown blue lotus, moon-faced, fond of peacock-feather ornaments, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, clad in beautiful yellow garments;
his body worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, surrounded by throngs of cows and cowherds—
I worship Govinda, who delights in playing the flute with its subtle notes and is adorned with divine limbs. || 3 ||
Oṃ!
Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Śrī, wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Viṣvaksena, the bestower of one's own perfection;
whose abode is the Ocean of Milk, the Lord of the Vyūhas, who reclines upon Śeṣa, and who is identical with the universe. || 1 ||
Accessible through devotion, the embodiment of the three forms, praised by the Earth oppressed by her burden, the God of gods, an ocean of compassion, the crest-jewel of all deities. || 2 ||
The source of happiness, the support of bliss, Mukunda, whose intention is joy;
changeless, yet the embodiment of action, he possesses the true nature of the inner self.
The inner self of all beings is characterized by the learned; his activity is for the purpose of protecting dharma.
He is the inner controller, whose form consists of the constituent parts [of time], and who is the witness of the divisions of time.
The remover of the earth's burden, intent on the instigation of Nārada, capable and celebrated by Nārada, he is devoted to the protection of the world. (5)
He who brought joy to the son of Rohiṇī, who enjoined him to the knowledge of yoga,
and who, possessing an ancient body and self-mastery, was cast into the interior of a great cave.
Śauri, the sole lord of the lineage of heroes, who caused the poison of fear to arise in Kaṃsa,
possessed a radiant power through Vasudeva and entered as the eighth embryo in Devakī.
The glorious Hari, son of Vasudeva and delighter of Devakī, possesses wondrous childhood; his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, and he has four arms.
His true nature is preeminent; he is born at the end of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, produced under the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), and arisen at the time of midnight.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, with eyes like lotuses,
wearing a crown, with the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, and adorned with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, with curly and arched locks of hair,
his ornaments clearly manifest, he was the ornament of the maternity chamber.
It destroys the darkness of the prison, indicates one's ancestors and former births, was praised by Vasudeva, is a hymn that wards off the threefold affliction. (12)
He is faultless, the embodiment of action, the ordainer of logical speech;
his movements are unseen, he is immutable, yet he has assumed a worldly form.
It gladdens the minds of the great seers, bestows auspiciousness upon the earth, satisfies the hosts of gods, and brings clarity to the hearts of the virtuous. || 14 ||
He who instructed Janaka on the means [of liberation], who was a festival for the eyes of Devakī, who was adorned by his father’s hand, and who deluded the guardian of the household; || 15 ||
He has opened all the doors by his own power, he is the bearer of his father,
he has the parasol of the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa, and he possesses the thousand names spoken by Śeṣa.
He who destroyed the flood of the Yamunā, who illuminated Vraja with his own radiance, who established the arrangement of self-knowledge, and who was born from the foremost of Yogamāyās. || 17 ||
Manifesting from the offering to Durgā, He who lies upon the bed of Yaśodā;
He whose splendor brings festival to Nanda the cowherd, and whose rising brings joy to Vraja. || 18 ||
The auspicious birth-rites were performed for the well-born one; he was delighted by the words of Gopībhadrā;
he feigned sleep and crushed the breast of Pūtanā. || 19 ||
He who took the life of the Putana who sought his breast-milk, who made the Putana cry out,
who was protected by the dust of the protective cow, and who was cherished in the hands of Yaśodā.
With the crown of his head kissed by Nandā, he who grants a happy rebirth to Pūtanā—
the Child, longing for sleep on his mother’s lap, with his toes placed in her mouth.
His eyes were as glossy as collyrium, his smiles blossomed in succession;
with playful glances and darting looks, he was the crusher of the demon Śakaṭāsura. || 22 ||
With auspicious blessings uttered by the twice-born, bathed in water purified by mantras,
resting on the lap of Yaśodā as his couch, he gazed into the face of Yaśodā.
Nourished by the breast-milk of Yaśodā, he was difficult to withstand for Tṛṇāvarta and others;
he was the destroyer of the demon Tṛṇāvarta and the cause of his mother's amazement. (24)
Having received an auspicious name, eager to walk about on his knees, with the jewel of his top-knot hanging down, he brought great joy to Ghoṣa and Gopa. || 25 ||
Seeking the reflection of his own face, his neck was marked by the glistening claws of a tiger;
he was beautiful with a coating of mud, and his hips were set upon fleshy thighs.
With his pair of knees rubbed raw, imitating the reflection [of the moon], his speech and activity characterized by indistinct sounds, and the emergence of his teeth visible through a smile; || 27 ||
Holding onto the hand of his nurse, with faltering and variegated steps,
he was accompanied by a suitable playmate and possessed the charming restlessness of childhood.
Drawn by the calf’s tail, he who was pulled by the calf’s tail forgot all other activities, bringing joy to the cowherds and cowherd girls. (29)
He who releases calves at the improper time, who smiles while being reviled in the cow-pen, who is a great thief of butter, and who gives food to children. || 30 ||
He kicked over the mortar and the pestle, broke the vessels of milk,
pulled down the hanging pots, and entered the dark interior of the house.
Richly adorned with the luster of precious jewels, yet rebuked and threatened by the cowherd girls;
his form grey with pollen, he was observed eating earth.
Beginning his speech with the talk of clay as told by a child, with his body hidden within his friend's [lap], his eyes restless with feigned alarm, he brought confidence to his mother;
with his face visible to his mother’s gaze, yet making all moving and non-moving things manifest through his mouth. (33)
His very self was cherished by Yaśodā; he himself was the deluder through his own sovereign will.
Clinging with affection to his mother, greedy for his mother’s breast,
bowing down in his request for fresh butter, he was a great consumer of fresh butter.
With his lips trembling from feigned anger, he gazes toward the courtyard of the assembly hall;
he is the breaker of the curd-churning jars, signaled by the tinkling of small bells.
A connoisseur of fresh butter, feigning tears while suspicious of theft, he recognized his mother’s exhaustion and was restrained by the tether of the rope. (37)
Bound by a rope, with trembling outer corners of his eyes, firmly tied to a mortar, dragged toward the mortar, Ananta was cursed by the son of Kubera. 38.
Reflecting upon the words of Nārada, he shattered the twin Arjuna trees;
praised by the son of Dhanada, he released Nanda from his bonds. || 39 ||
Delighting in the songs sung by children, finding joy in the tossing of arms,
self-knowing, under the influence of his friends, he is the source of the virtues celebrated in the songs of the cowherd girls.
Mounted upon a cart for his journey, making his abode in Vṛndāvana,
he is single-mindedly intent on tending the calves of the cows, accompanied by various implements for his pastimes.
Delighting in the throwing of projectiles, he was skilled in the playing of the flute;
he imitated the lowing of bulls and mimicked the sound of a bull. || 42 ||
Delighted by the play of wrestling, he imitated the warbling of the cuckoo;
adopting the gait of a swan, he mimicked the movements of every living creature.
He who resembles a bee, who [consumed] curd-rice and rice-porridge, who was preceded by a calf, who was powerful, who seized the demon Baka, and who scorched the palate of Baka. 44.
He who was called upon by the frightened cowherd boys, who tore open the beak of Baka;
the enemy of the demon Baka, the cowherd, the child who brings about wonders for the young. 45.
Embraced by Balabhadra, he made his dwelling in playful sport;
he was a knower of the foundations of the bridge of play, a wondrous leaper like a monkey.
Playing with balls, his experiences of existence such as joy and so forth having ceased,
his head adorned with flowers, he carried a basket of sweet and succulent food.
He was draped with hanging clusters of *guñjā* berries,
dressed in a garland of peacock feathers, fond of forest food, and making calves low by blowing through a horn.
He wears a charming crest-ornament of sprouts and flowers, with bees drawn by their fragrance; his feet possess anklets that produce a sweet jingling sound, and he wears bracelets on his wrists.
Teaching one another, skilled in play, and supremely deceitful;
delighted by echoes, it moves with agility through the branches. (50)

The destroyer of the demons Agha and Dānava, the annihilator of obstacles for Vraja, the restorer of life to Vraja, a treasure-house of auspiciousness, and the bestower of liberation upon the demons. || 51 ||
Seated upon the sandy bank of the Kālindī, having eaten together with the children of Vraja,
he holds his flute tucked under his arm or against his belly, acting like a cowherd boy.
With his horned staff resting in the crook of his arm, possessing a pure smile,
holding a morsel of curd-rice in his left hand, and speaking with sweet, gentle words.
With a fruit placed between his fingers, he is supremely purifying;
seeking the calf that remains invisible, he removes the fear of the cowherd boys.
Not seeing the herdsmen and their calves, and having realized the full extent of his divine power,
he whose form is that of the Supreme Person (Virāṭpuruṣa) went in search of the calves and the cowherds.
He possesses objects corresponding to his own volition, assuming the forms of both calf and cow;
he manifests in the manner of the calf's activities and is stationed in his proper place.
Having the form of a child of the Vraja, happily drinking the milk of the cows and the gopīs,
he has long since become reddish-brown, self-controlled, and one who has realized the majesty of Brahman.
Possessing manifold powers, he is the protector of the cowherd boys and the calves released by the serpent;
he causes shame to Brahmā, is praised by the Creator (Dhātṛ), and is the accomplisher of all goals.
Brahman is composed of Brahman, unmanifest, consisting of splendor, and blissful in nature;
he is the etymology, the manifestation, the manifest, and the meditation that is without support.
He is the sovereign lord, devoid of a physical body, assuming forms for the sake of the divine hosts;
he is free from desire, the source of all the Vedas, and possesses both subtle and gross forms.
Pervasive and that which is pervaded, the agent of compassion, esteemed for his diverse conduct;
consisting of the Vedic meters, the self of primordial matter (pradhāna), possessing the dual form of both the manifest and the unmanifest. || 61 ||
Possessing manifold forms, free from anger, supreme, primordial nature, and beyond sequence; endowed with all coverings, the god of all, Maheśvara. || 62 ||
Possessing great majesty as before, he showed himself as a calf; Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd of the Yādavas, brought joy to the assembly of cowherds.

Brahmā was delighted by his smiling glance; he is fond of the words of those devoted to him and dear to them; his feet are washed by tears of the bliss of Brahman; and he is skilled in the manifold variety of his divine play.
With his heart solely devoted to Balabhadra, having caused the name [of Kṛṣṇa] to be invoked throughout Gokula,
this noble cowherd boy wore a rope as his sacred thread.
His fatigue dispelled by the shade of a tree, with the lap of a cowherd as his pillow,
his feet massaged by cowherds, fanned by the fans of cowherds;
awakened by the pleasant singing of cowherds, he was a friend cherished by Śrīdāman.
He is the singular soul of his friend Sunanda, and he delights Subala with his very life.
He who sports in the groves of palm trees, who overthrew Dhenuka with his strength,
who is cherished by the good fortune of the cowherd girls, and whose locks of hair are sprinkled with the dust of the cows.
Afflicted by the pain of separation from the gopīs, having performed his ablutions with the gopīs,
he possessed long, powerful arms and wore a full-blown white lotus as an ear-ornament.
His gaze was playful, charming, and smiling within its depths;
he was richly adorned with garlands, ornaments, and unguents, and he ate food offered by his mother.
Reclining on his excellent bed, delighted by conversations of love with Rādhā, wandering along the banks of the Yamunā, he brings joy to the Vraja community afflicted by sorrow. (71)
He who generates fear in the serpent Kāliya, he who is surrounded by a multitude of aged snakes,
he who is the dancer upon the stage of the hoods of the serpent Kāliya, and the crusher of Kāliya.
Delighted by the praise of the Naga wives, he bestows prosperity through various forms;
the Lord of the Self has an all-pervading gaze, and he is fond of the self-praise of those who behold him.
The Lord of all, possessing all virtues, renowned as the leader of all Sātvatas;
his power unimpeded, his gaze like that of the moon and sun, and pure as the sky.
He whose gait is indescribable; who grants alms to the husband of the Naga women;
whose head bears the imprint of the mark of his own foot upon the king of serpents; and who was praised by Kāliya. 75.
Fearless, with eyes on all sides, praised for his supreme qualities, the Lord;
I am the Self, the vital breath of the Maruts, the Supreme Self, whose head is the sky. (76)
His soul delighted by the offerings of the cowherds, having driven away the serpent Kāliya from the lake,
he engaged in pleasant conversation with Balabhadra and found bliss in the embrace of the cowherd women.

The protector of cowherds who were terrified by the forest fire, the extinguisher of the forest fire, one addicted to the game of covering the eyes, and one whose conduct is like that of a king. || 78 ||
Wearing the side-locks of youth, gentle, and fond of sporting with his army;
he who struck down the irrepressible Pralamba and is devoted to those who possess strength. || 79 ||
He is the quencher of the fire in the Muñja forest, the one who finds delight in the rainy season;
he is the destroyer of the Daityas who rested upon a rock and whose seat was the green grass.
Constantly sung of by the trusted gopīs, wearing a karṇikāra flower as an ear-ornament,
dressed in the attire of a dancer, marked with a lotus garland, and surrounded by the gopīs.
The corners of his eyes captivated the hearts of the gopīs;
he was intent on playing the flute, his lotus-face resting [upon it], producing beautiful sounds from his mouth. || 82 ||
With a magnificent flute placed against his bimba-red lips, he enchants the entire universe;
his flute-playing, praised by the people of Vraja, is melodious and dear to the ears.
Desiring to take birth as a cowherd among the cowherds and cowherdesses, he was saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and others;
he was like a flood of rivers of songs and hymns of praise, and he caused the peacocks to dance with his sound.
A tree trunk sprouting with passion, a tree bent by songs;
a deer who has forgotten to chew his mouthful of grass, lured by another deer. (85)

He was a remover of the natural enmity of tigers and other predators toward their prey, a sweet singer whose songs caused the calves to prance with ears erect at the intense outpouring of love from the herds of cows.
Beheld by Brahmā and others who have attained the motionless vehicle, he is saluted by the entire universe;
the flocks of birds with outstretched wings cause the clouds to appear like parasols.
He is gracious, supreme bliss, and the one who has painted the moving and the unmoving;
he is the lover of the cowherd women, marked by the saffron from the breasts of the gopīs.

Delighted by the water-sports of the cowherd girls, he stripped off the garments of the gopīs; with garlands of cowherds placed upon his shoulders and a smile like the kunda flower, he stood there. (89)

The moon to the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, whose garments were requested by the gopīs, the one who grants salutations from the gopīs, and he who is saluted with single-minded devotion by the gopīs. || 90 ||
Seeking the special offering of the cowherd girls' joined palms, enticed by the play of the cowherds, He—
whose garments are peaceful yet who makes the cowherd girls' folded hands tremble— is the destroyer of sins.

Seeking the playful amorous sports of the gopīs, the fulfiller of all the desires of the gopīs, the giver of garments to the cowherd women, the stealer of the hearts of the gopīs, and full of curiosity. 92.

He is the beloved of Vṛndāvana, the kinsman of the cowherds, the performer of sacrifices, the one who does not accept food offered without being invited, the Lord of Sacrifice, the knower of the essence of sacrifice, and the one desired by the wife of the sacrificer. || 93 ||
Satiated by the food offered by the wives of sages, he is fond of the wives of sages;
he understands the feelings of the wives of the twice-born and bestows boons upon the wives of the twice-born.

He bestows liberation upon those whose virtue has been obstructed; he deludes the twice-born; he grants the wisdom of sages; he is praised by sacrificers; and he is the knower of the sacrifice of Indra.
He was the one who prevented the sacrifice of Śakra performed according to the rites prescribed by his father;
he caused indignation in Śakra and was intent upon quelling the rain sent by Śakra.
The upholder of Govardhana, intent on protecting the multitude of cowherds and cows, he who used the arm-bar of the formidable staff of Mount Govardhana as a parasol. 97.
For seven days he bore the king of mountains, destroying the pride of him whose vehicle is the clouds; Acyuta placed the mountain-king upon the tips of his arms.
The mountain was established in its own place, honored with offerings of yogurt and sesame seeds by the cowherd girls;
it was gladdened by the rain of flowers from the well-disposed minds [of the gods] and saluted by Indra.
Sprinkled with the milk-filled waters of the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, praised by Surabhi,
having the earth as his feet and medicinal herbs as his hair, he is the protector of dharma and is composed of mind.
He who delights in the sacrifice of knowledge, the eye of the scriptures, and the charioteer of all purposes;
the omnipresent Lord who was bathed by the celestial Gaṅgā brought down from the sky by the trunk of Airāvata. 101.

Consecrated by Brahmā, the protector of the cows, the bringer of auspiciousness to all the worlds, consisting of all the Vedas, the seeker of the bliss of those who have immersed themselves [in yoga], and the beloved of the ancestors. 102.

He who takes delight in self-inspection as proclaimed by Varuṇa, he who is worshipped by Varuṇa, he whose progenitor was brought by Varuṇa, and he who knows his own majesty through the cowherds. || 103 ||
He bestows the three goals of life upon the multitude of cowherds who rejoice in the light of his own world;
he is hidden within the heart of Brahmā, the beholder of the cowherds, and the bestower of the state of Brahman.

Delighting in dwelling like the autumn moon, the Lord of Śrī, who is capable of bringing others under his control, the remover of fear, he remains the object of the Gopīs' meditation while their husbands keep them confined. 105.
He who is to be tasted by the eyes of the gopīs, who finds bliss in the playful words of the gopīs,
who removes the pride of the gopīs, and who is the leader of hundreds of herds of gopīs.
Adorned with the Vaijayantī garland, the increaser of the pride of the Gopīs, the excellent instructor of the beloveds of the cowherds, the lover who is the destroyer of the God of Love himself. 107.
Having offered betel to his own self, his excellent youth having borne fruit, his eyes fixed upon the breasts of the cowherd maidens, he was moved by the love of the cowherd maidens. 108.
Seated upon the hem of a gopī’s garment, he is the bee to the lotus-eyes of the gopīs;
he is intent on the rāsa dance and the ornament of the circle of gopīs. || 109 ||
Resplendent as the central sapphire amidst a row of cowherd girls' golden jewels,
he is the moon among the Vidyādharas, the destroyer of the curse, and the one who severed the head of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
The sinless one whose strength was fully gratified by the crest-jewel of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
the creator of misfortune for his enemies and the slayer of the wicked Daitya Keśin.
With a face smiling with joy, steady yet agitated by separation, his love was offered to Saṅkarṣaṇa, and he became the object of Akrūra’s meditation. || 112 ||

Praised by Akrūra, hidden, characterized by the function of the qualities (guṇas), accessible through the means of valid cognition, consisting of those [qualities] alone as its composite whole, and intent upon the intellect (buddhi). || 113 ||
He is the one who has crushed all means of valid cognition, the establisher of all perceptions,
the Puruṣa whose essence is Pradhāna, and whose vision is distorted by error.
He who is beheld by Madhurāja, the repeller of washermen;
he who is clothed in variegated garments and bestows boons upon the excellent garland-makers. || 115 ||
The liberator of Kubjā from her crookedness, the bestower of youth upon Kubjā, fragrant with the unguents of Kubjā’s limbs, and the shatterer of Kaṃsa’s bow. 116.
The steadfast one, the crusher of Kuvalayāpīḍa, the instiller of fear in Kaṃsa;
armed with the tusks of elephants, the terrifier in the arena, and skilled in wrestling.
The slayer of Cāṇūra, the enemy of Kaṃsa, the bestower of joy upon Devakī;
he who bows at the feet of Vasudeva and the liberator of his paternal kinsmen. || 118 ||

O King, you are the remover of the fears of the vast earth; you are the bestower of sovereignty upon Ugrasena; you are the Lord of Śacī abiding by your command; and you are capable of bringing forth the Sudharmā assembly hall.
The first was a benefactor of the twice-born and a demonstrator of the conduct of the learned;
he was a wise man whose singular focus was the practice of the sciences mastered under Sāndīpani.
Skilled in performing the beloved rites of his guru, he was worshipped by the western ocean; having slain Pañcajana, he obtained the Pāñcajanya conch, and he was honored by Yama.
The son of the Guru brought by Dharmarāja’s victory, the wide-striding one;
the teacher who bestows the son of the Guru, the member of Madhurāja’s assembly. || 122 ||
Worthy of worship by the son of Jamadagni, he wanders upon Mount Gomanta;
he is the quencher of the forest fire on Gomanta, and his ornaments were brought by Garuḍa.
Resplendent with his discus and other weapons, he removed the pride of Jarāsaṃdha;
he was the slayer of King Sṛgāla and the bestower of the kingdom upon Sṛgāla’s son.
He who utterly destroyed the Kālayavana demon, who granted boons to Mucukunda, who commanded the great ocean, and who planned the city of Dvārakā. 125.
Dwelling in Dvārakā, the destroyer of Rukmin’s pride, the leader of the Yadus,
the radiant husband of Rukmiṇī, the progenitor of Pradyumna, and the Lord.
He who has removed the suffering of the three worlds, whose grandfather is Aniruddha,
who seeks the station of Aniruddha, the wielder of the discus, whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
He was the destroyer of the city of Bāṇāsura, the conqueror of the fire-engines used for protection,
the one who quelled the fury of the Pramathas, and the vanquisher of the fever of Maheśvara.
The conqueror of the power of the six chakras, the deluder of spirits and vetālas; the subduer of Śambhu’s trident, the one who causes Śambhu to expand, and he who is praised by Śambhu. || 129 ||
He whose self is the senses, whose heart is the moon, the Lord of all lords of yoga;
he whose heart is Hiraṇyagarbha, who turns back the whirlpool of delusion. || 130 ||

He is the treasure-trove of self-knowledge, the intellect, and the storehouse; he possesses the form of the subtle elements alone; he has Indra and Agni as his faces; he has Time as his navel; and he traverses the paths of all the scriptures.

The witness of all cognitions in the fourth state (turīya), dwelling far from the self that delights in dualities; he whose further shore is unknown, who holds sovereignty over Śrī, and whose abode is the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 132 ||
The lamp of the self, whose nature is pure consciousness, the abode of glory;
the cutter of the forest of Bāṇa’s arms, the increaser of Mahendra’s joy. || 133 ||

He who knows the cessation of the unceasing, who brought the cowherd community from the lord of waters, the hero who conquered the lord of waters, the victor in battle, and the solicitor of jewels. || 134 ||
He was intent on searching for Prasena, the giver of the jewel to Jāmbavān, the captor of the daughter of the king of bears, and the beloved of Jāmbavatī. || 135 ||
The beloved of Satyabhāmā, the fulfiller of desires, the slayer of Śatadhanvan’s head; the lord of Kālindī, the kinsman of Akrūra, and the bestower of jewels upon Akrūra. 136.
The beloved of Kaikeyī, the husband of Bhadrā, the lord of Nāgnajitī, the captivator of Mādrī, the life-partner of Śaibyā, and the one of vast strides.
The beloved of Suśīlā, a great festival for the eyes of Mitravindā, the husband of Lakṣmaṇā, who besieged the great city of Prāgjyotiṣa. 138.
Murāri, the destroyer of the snare and enclosure of the gods, skilled in fierce combat, the one who took away the head of Hayagrīva, the soul of all, and the seer of all. || 139 ||
The destroyer of the demon Naraka, the bestower of the kingdom upon the son of Naraka;
praised by the Earth, the radiant soul, the beloved one who grants the fruit of sacrifice. || 140 ||
He is the grasper of virtues, the beholder of virtues, whose own self is hidden, and who possesses sovereign power;
he is the poet, the overseer of the world, and the embodiment of the supreme imperishable.
The protector of those who have sought refuge, the garlanded one, the great increaser of Brahman;
he whose meaning consists of the power of the signified and the signifier, the bestower of perfection upon all that is manifested. || 142 ||
He is self-luminous, beyond description, self-manifesting, and eternal; he is the essence of sound, the lord of ten million mantras, and the one who brings an end to manifold doctrines.
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others;
who has transformed the host of gods into immortals, and who liberated the maiden from her bonds.
Lord of sixteen thousand women, beloved, the source of desire for his beloveds, the stealer of the mountain of jewels for play, adorned with the parasol of Varuṇa. (145)
He was saluted by Śakra; he gave his earrings to the mother of Śakra; he was praised by Aditi; and his consciousness was proclaimed by the Brahmins. || 146 ||
The Purāṇa is self-restrained, unstained by birth, the twenty-sixth principle, and the bestower of wealth; it is the policy for fame, devoid of beginning and end, and fond of sacred narratives. 147.
The awakening of Brahman, supreme bliss, the stealer of the Pārijāta tree, the destroyer of Pauṇḍraka’s life, and the slayer of the King of Kāśī. || 148 ||
The subduer of Kṛtyā’s pride, consecrated for the slaying of Cakra;
the destroyer of Kaṃsa, the father of Sāmba, and the crusher of the Ḍimbhakas.
The sage, the protector, the bestower of boons upon his father, consecrated for the sacrifice;
the charioteer, the director of the charioteers, Phālguna, the beloved of the month of Phālguna. || 150 ||
Hari, who caused the seven oceans to be solidified and was the one who split the seven oceans;
the self-luminous one of perfect glory, beheld by the primordial Nārāyaṇa. (151)
He is the bestower of sons upon brahmins and the giver of sons to all mothers;
he causes wonder in Arjuna and awakens Arjuna to the meaning of the Praṇava. || 152 ||
Intent on a journey to Kailāsa, he was the ornament of the Badarī hermitage;
being fond of his devotees, he was pleased by Ghaṇṭākarṇa’s devotion despite the latter’s ignorance.
He is to be meditated upon by hosts of sages and others; he is the bestower of boons upon Ghaṇṭākarṇa;
he is devoted to the practice of asceticism, clothed in bark garments, and bears tawny matted locks. 154.
He had directly perceived the Lord of Beings; he was a singer of praises to Śiva and was himself praised by Śiva;
he was curious to witness Kṛṣṇā’s svayaṃvara and was esteemed by all. 155.
The subduer of the onset of Bala, who revealed his power to the Pāṇḍavas;
the bestower of what Arjuna desired while he was in the guise of an ascetic; the one whose range is the self of all. 156.
The one who performed the marriage of Subhadrā and Phālguna; the one who gladdened Phālguna;
the radiant one who gratified [Agni] at Khāṇḍava; the liberator of the Dānava Maya. 157.

It was easy for him to command Yudhiṣṭhira, who was worthy of the Rājasūya sacrifice; it was easy for him to afflict Jarāsaṃdha with Bhīma; and it was easy for him to bestow the kingdom upon the son of the King of Magadha. 158.

The liberator from royal captivity, the one honored foremost in the Rājasūya sacrifice, the one who could not endure the King of Cedi and others, the one praised by Bhīṣma, and the elder brother of the Sātvatas. 159.
The gatherer of all self-interests, the sustainer of Mount Mandara, the incarnation of sacrifice, and the fulfiller of Prahlāda’s vow. || 160 ||
The destroyer of Bali’s sacrifice and the assembly hall, the ender of the arrogant kṣatriya clans,
the slayer of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, the conqueror, and the beloved of Revatī’s affection.
The presiding authority over all incarnations, the deluder of those outside the Vedas, the remover of the defects of the Kali age, the one of ten names, and the firm in his vows. (162)
The immeasurable self, the Lord of the universe, the eloquent one, the slayer of the King of Cedi, he for whom Draupadī composed a hymn of praise—Keśava, the Supreme Person. 163.
Nārāyaṇa, Madhupati, Mādhava, the one free from defects; Govinda, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana. || 164 ||
Trivikrama, Lord of the three worlds, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Puruṣa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, Padmanābha, and Mahāhrada. || 165 ||
Dāmodara, the fourfold manifestation, the protector of Pāñcālī, the slayer of Śālva, the one praised in battle, and the destroyer of Dantavakra. (166)
He is the dear friend of Dāmodara and is fond of tasting flattened rice.
Compassionate Dāmodara, the bestower of prosperity, who looks again upon the gopīs. || 167 ||
The victorious yogi who grants liberation to the cowherd girls, who brought satisfaction to Durvāsas, and who remained unrecognized while observing the Pāṇḍavas gathered in Vraja. 168.
Devoted to Pārthasārathi, wise, acting as an envoy for the Pāṇḍavas, satisfied by the hospitality of Vidura, and bestowing contentment upon Kuntī. || 169 ||
The scorner of Suyodhana, the knower of Duryodhana’s transformations, eternally praised by Vidura, the scion of the Vṛṣṇi clan, whose nature is auspicious. 170.
The Lord of the twenty-five principles, who possesses a body consisting of the twenty-four [tattvas], is the benefactor of all and is eternally worshipped by the Śārṅgins. || 171 ||
Inconceivable, with a sweet voice, appearing as a virtuous man yet difficult to approach,
he followed human customs while observing the destruction of the Kaurava lord.
Upendra, the enemy of the Dānavas, praised by the great, and possessed of great luster;
the god who is devoted to the Brahmanas, learned in the Vedas, and whose intent is the welfare of cows and Brahmanas. (173)
He was of excellent character, auspicious in his undertakings, possessed of the embodiment of perfect wisdom, pure by nature, a true friend, a worthy refuge, and endowed with noble marks.
Bestowing his gaze upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he pierced Karna;
holding the goad, he caused Dhananjaya to forget his own universal form.
He who is fond of Sāman chanting, the cow of dharma, the best of castes, the imperishable;
the performer of the rites of the four ages, the revealer of the universal form. || 176 ||
He whose purpose is the protection of the awakening of Brahman; he who bears the wheel for the sake of Bhīṣma;
he who destroys the distress of Arjuna; he who is adorned with the fangs of Time. || 177 ||
Possessing the infinite majesty of Sujātā, he caused Arjuna to act as if in a dream;
he brought about an untimely twilight and placed the sun within his discus.
The crusher of the wicked, the fulfiller of Pārtha’s vow, he who spoke of the place where the head of the King of Sindhu would fall, and the one possessed of discerning vision. (179)
He removed Subhadrā’s grief, was astonished by Droṇa’s arrogance, dispelled Arjuna’s resentment, and brought joy to the Pāṇḍavas. (180)
The chariot of the son of Kuntī was pressed down by his big toe; he was the conqueror of the serpent’s head, the pacifier of Kāla’s wrath, and the bestower of victory upon Bhīmasena. || 181 ||
Having slain Aśvatthāman, the skillful son of Pāṇḍu was free from fear;
he neutralized the *iṣīkā* weapon and investigated the protection of Droṇa’s son. 182.
The unyielding crest-jewel of the son of Droṇa was snatched away by the son of Pṛthā;
meanwhile, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was filled with pride at the sight of Bhīma’s retaliation.
Bestower of wisdom upon Bhīṣma, peaceful, with a face like the autumnal moon, the elder brother of Gada, and the fulfiller of the Pāñcālī's vow. 184.

The son of Dharma, protected from the sight of Gāndhārī’s anger, is free from ailment; he is the dispeller of the fear and distress of those who seek refuge, and he brings about the extraction of the dart of Bhīṣma.
Śāntanu’s son was peaceful, absorbed in all dharmas that have been fully aroused;
he delighted Pārtha by reminding him of the meaning of the Brahma-vidyā, and he was a master of great weapons.
Supremely noble in his graciousness, he bestows a happy rebirth upon the son of Gaṅgā;
he brings about the destruction of the faction of adversaries and protects the lives of those who have been examined. || 187 ||
The teacher of the world, who initiated the horse sacrifice for the son of Dharma,
having received due honor for the fulfillment of his purpose, remained there for one month and then departed.
He who bestowed joy upon Uttaṅka by revealing his own divine form,
who made Janaka understand the entire Bhārata as he had spoken it, and who is the creator of all beings.
Unable to endure the excess of the Ādavas, he performed the worship of his elders and other venerable ones.
Samudrasthāpita, Aścaryamusalī, and Vṛṣṇivāhaka. || 190 ||
Armed with the sage’s curse as his weapon, he had been entreated by the gods led by Brahmā;
now eager to withdraw the rain and longing to return to his own abode, he departed.
Diligent in the manifestation of radiant light, he creates various kinds of signs;
he is to be served by all the Yādavas and possesses the most excellent retinue. || 192 ||
Wandering through the groves on the shore, his fatigue removed by the coastal breeze,
the Yādava Ananta— the very soul of Time— was pleased in mind by their hymns of praise.
Delighted by the sight of the twice-born, he was a great festival for holy pilgrimage sites;
he gladdened all the Brahmins with hospitable honors and was beloved by the gods.
Having bathed at sacred fords, he was meritorious, the bestower of merit, and the purifier of holy sites;
he gifted ten million cows to Brahmins and gave away hundreds of millions of gold pieces.
Deluded by his own māyā, the hero of all the Vṛṣṇis, though a knower of distinctions,
became the one who pointed out the lotus-weaponed [Viṣṇu] as a Yādava possessed by his own self.
The bestower of desired boons to the deities, having accomplished his purpose, with a serene mind,
possessing the steady strength of ten thousand Śeṣas, and gazed upon by a thousand hooded serpents.
Seated in the excellent shade of the Brahma-tree, established in the lotus posture,
the inner self, whose nature is the ultimate reality, was intent upon profound meditation.
He whose feet are worshipped by Vyādhi and Vidhya, who liberated the Niṣādas from fear, who was delighted by the praise of Pulinda, and who granted a favorable rebirth to Pulinda. || 199 ||
The Lord spoke words concerning the tasks to be performed by Arjuna and others as directed by Daruka;
accompanied by divine drums, he was honored by a rain of flowers. || 200 ||
The ancient Supreme Lord, the fullness of plenitude, praised by all;
the primordial Master, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest. (201)
The glorious Supreme Self, higher than the highest—*oṃ namaḥ*. This is the declaration of the fruit: this thousand names of Kṛṣṇa bestows all goals.
The Blessed One, whose form is without interval, [taught] at the beginning to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
It was proclaimed by him to Vasiṣṭha; then Parāśara received it from him and proclaimed it to Vyāsa; Śuka obtained it from Vyāsa. (203)
It was proclaimed on earth by his many disciples during the Dvāpara age;
and by the command of Kṛṣṇa, the omnipresent Lord Harihara made it renowned in the Kali age.
Whoever recites this with devotion and listens to it with a concentrated mind, the deities of sacred fords, holy sites, and other such places will pray to him for their own success. (205)
Those sins which cannot be removed by all the various penances without exception perish through praising him even once.
By reciting this, one shall obtain the fruit belonging to the sage who is liberated from the three debts, who follows the Śruti and Smṛti, and whose form is the Trinity.
Whoever recites or hears this thousand names shall obtain the fruit of consecrating a thousand Śiva-liṅgas. || 208 ||
Having muttered this, the victorious Kirīṭin, who wields the Pāśupata weapon and is the very life-breath of Kṛṣṇa, obtained Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer. (209)
By means of this recitation, Draupadī, Damayantī, Sāvitrī, and Suśīlā conquered their misfortunes and obtained their desires. (210)
What need is there for much speaking? A human being, filled with joy while praising this, shall attain the bliss of Brahman at the end and achieve union with Kṛṣṇa. || 211 ||
The Hymn of the Thousand Names of Kṛṣṇa is complete.
